books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, D. Gender and Family Roles in the Age of the Market Revolution

stimulus.text: Harriet Martineau, an English visitor, wrote in Society in America (1837): “If a test of civilisation be sought, none can be so sure as the condition of that half of society over which the other half has power.” She added: “The Americans have, in the treatment of women, fallen below, not only their own democratic principles, but the practice of some parts of the Old World.” Martineau also wrote that “the sum and substance of female education in America, as in England, is training women to consider marriage as the sole object in life.”
stimulus.source_note: Harriet Martineau, Society in America (1837), chapter “Woman.” Verbatim quotations verified against the Quotidiana transcription of the 1837 text.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Martineau's criticism points most directly to which legal reality for married women in the period?

options.text: Women could vote in most states if they owned property
options.misconception: Women could not vote; Beecher herself says women's interests are entrusted to men without women voting.

options.text: Under feme covert, a wife's property became her husband's
Women could serve on juries in the new western states
options.misconception: Women could not sit on juries anywhere in this period.

options.text: Married women kept their wages under the protection of the courts
options.misconception: Under feme covert a married woman had no separate property, so her wages belonged to her husband.

rationales.A: No state let women vote in this period. The vote was for white men, and Martineau's complaint is exactly that women had no share in it.
rationales.B: Martineau's charge that women are the half without power points to the law. Under feme covert, a married woman's property became her husband's, and she had no legal standing of her own.
rationales.C: Juries were for men only. Women could neither vote nor sit on juries.
rationales.D: A married woman under feme covert owned nothing separate from her husband. Her wages were his in law.
rationales.general:
1. Turn her charge into a question. What law made women the half without power?
2. Recall the doctrine. Under feme covert, a wife had no independent legal or political standing.
3. Check the details. Her property became her husband's, and she could not vote or sit on a jury.
Background: The law also gave wives no protection against physical abuse by their husbands, and denied them a vote.
Remember: when a writer charges a whole society, look for the law that makes the charge true.
